notes: r6's ui-yaml-expansion-defaults tests the UI default alone to keep the card to one fact.

cards.statement: `workflow:rules` controls whether GitLab creates a pipeline for a particular triggering event.
cards.explanation: GitLab applies workflow rules before selecting the jobs that would belong to the pipeline.

cards.statement: `workflow:rules` supports `when: manual` for a user to start the pipeline.
cards.explanation: GitLab accepts `always` and `never` as the `when` values in `workflow:rules`. Manual scheduling applies to jobs.
cards.misconception: Workflow rules accept the same scheduling values as job rules.

cards.statement: A matching `workflow:rules:variables` value overrides the same top-level YAML variable.
cards.explanation: GitLab uses the matching workflow rule's value instead of the top-level YAML default for that name.

cards.statement: `workflow:name` can combine fixed text with CI/CD variable values.
cards.explanation: GitLab expands variable references when assigning the configured pipeline name.

cards.statement: `CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE` is `push` for pipelines created by pushing tags.
cards.explanation: The `push` source covers tag creation through a push as well as pushes to branches.

cards.statement: GitLab sets `CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE` to `api` for a pipeline started with New pipeline in the project UI.
cards.explanation: A pipeline started with New pipeline in the project UI has `CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE` set to `web`.
cards.misconception: Starting a pipeline from the project UI gives it the API pipeline source.

source.title: Specify when jobs run with rules

cards.statement: `CI_COMMIT_BRANCH` contains the source branch name in merge request pipelines.
cards.explanation: `CI_COMMIT_BRANCH` is available in branch pipelines but unavailable in merge request pipelines.
cards.misconception: Merge request pipelines expose their source branch through CI_COMMIT_BRANCH.

cards.statement: `include:rules` can use job-only predefined variables to select configuration files.
cards.explanation: Job-only predefined variables arrive when a runner takes a job. `include:rules` uses pre-pipeline predefined variables.
cards.misconception: Job-only variables are available when GitLab evaluates conditional includes.

cards.statement: `workflow:rules` can suppress branch pipelines when `CI_OPEN_MERGE_REQUESTS` has a value.
cards.explanation: GitLab's workflow example rejects a branch pipeline when that branch has an open merge request, avoiding duplicate pipelines.

cards.statement: GitLab marks an empty push pipeline created by a `[ci skip]` commit message as successful.
cards.explanation: GitLab still creates an empty pipeline for the skipped push and gives it the Skipped status.
cards.misconception: Skipping a push pipeline gives the empty pipeline a successful status.

cards.statement: The `ci.skip` push option can skip merge request pipelines associated with the push.
cards.explanation: The `ci.skip` push option skips push pipelines and leaves associated merge request pipelines eligible to run.
cards.misconception: The ci.skip push option also skips merge request pipelines.

cards.statement: GitLab uses the schedule owner's permissions for automatic scheduled pipeline runs.
cards.explanation: The schedule owner supplies the access level used for automatic scheduled runs.

cards.statement: A job's YAML variable overrides a top-level variable with the same name.
cards.explanation: A job-level YAML value customizes that job. Other jobs keep the same-named top-level default unless they override it too.

cards.statement: A job's `variables: {}` preserves variables defined at the top level.
cards.explanation: An empty job variables map suppresses top-level YAML variable defaults.
cards.misconception: An empty job variables map leaves top-level defaults available.

cards.statement: GitLab hides YAML variable values from users with read access to the project's repository.
cards.explanation: YAML variable values are visible to users who can read the repository containing `.gitlab-ci.yml`.
cards.misconception: GitLab conceals variable values stored in the pipeline YAML file.

cards.statement: A project's Developer role can edit CI/CD variables in the project's settings.
cards.explanation: Changing project CI/CD variables requires the Maintainer role or higher.
cards.misconception: The Developer role grants permission to manage project CI/CD variables.

cards.statement: GitLab gives the closest subgroup's variable precedence over a same-named parent-group variable.
cards.explanation: An inherited group variable comes from the nearest subgroup that defines its name, rather than a more distant ancestor.

cards.statement: On GitLab Self-Managed, the group Owner role grants permission to create instance CI/CD variables.
cards.explanation: Creating instance CI/CD variables requires administrator access on GitLab Self-Managed.
cards.misconception: The group Owner role grants authority over instance CI/CD variables.

cards.statement: GitLab gives project variables higher precedence than same-named job-level YAML variables.
cards.explanation: A value in project CI/CD settings takes priority over a job's YAML value, even when the YAML declares it inside that job.

cards.statement: GitLab gives a project variable precedence over a same-named variable from a dotenv report.
cards.explanation: A dotenv value does not replace a same-named project variable, even when a preceding job generates the report.

source.title: Pass dotenv variables to specific jobs

cards.statement: A manual job uses the user's job variables ahead of same-named pipeline variables.
cards.explanation: Variables entered when starting a manual job outrank existing pipeline variables, so the entered value wins a name collision.

cards.statement: Multi-project triggers passing variables use the upstream Minimum role to use pipeline variables setting.
cards.explanation: For a multi-project trigger that passes variables, GitLab checks the user's downstream role against the downstream project's Minimum role to use pipeline variables setting.
cards.misconception: The upstream project controls the role restriction for variables passed to a multi-project pipeline.

cards.statement: A job receives the stored contents as the environment value of a file type CI/CD variable.
cards.explanation: For a file type CI/CD variable, GitLab sets the environment value to the path of a temporary file containing the stored value.
cards.misconception: A file type variable exposes the stored contents directly as its environment value.

cards.statement: Since GitLab 18.6, GitLab leaves Expand variable reference off for new UI variables by default.
cards.explanation: Values such as `$OTHER_VAR` stay literal until the creator enables Expand variable reference.
cards.volatilityNote: GitLab may change the default expansion setting for newly created UI variables.

cards.statement: Since GitLab 18.1, a project setting lets eligible merge request pipelines read protected variables.
cards.explanation: A merge request pipeline gets protected variables when the project allows access, both branches are protected in the same project, and its triggering user can push or merge to the target branch.

cards.statement: Since GitLab 18.3, GitLab selects Masked by default for new CI/CD variables created in the UI.
cards.explanation: GitLab starts a new UI variable with Masked visibility; its creator can select a different visibility.
cards.volatilityNote: GitLab may change the default visibility of newly created UI variables.

cards.statement: A Maintainer can block malicious job scripts from reading a variable by choosing Masked visibility.
cards.explanation: Masking redacts matching values in logs. A job's script still has access to the variable's value.
cards.misconception: Masking prevents malicious scripts from accessing a secret.

cards.statement: A Maintainer can switch an existing variable's visibility to Masked and hidden.
cards.explanation: A creator chooses Masked and hidden when adding a variable. GitLab prevents changing an existing variable to hidden.
cards.misconception: Existing variables can be converted to hidden variables.

cards.statement: A pipeline running in a fork reads the parent project's CI/CD variables by default.
cards.explanation: A pipeline running in a fork uses the fork's variables rather than the parent project's variables.
cards.misconception: Fork pipelines inherit CI/CD variables from their parent project.

cards.statement: GitLab keeps CI_JOB_TOKEN valid until the pipeline finishes.
cards.explanation: GitLab revokes CI_JOB_TOKEN when its job finishes, even if other jobs keep the pipeline running.
cards.misconception: A job token remains usable for the lifetime of its pipeline.

cards.statement: CI_JOB_TOKEN uses the access level of the user who starts the job.
cards.explanation: A job token receives its triggering user's access level for the GitLab resources available to job tokens.

cards.statement: Since GitLab 19.0, GitLab issues CI/CD job tokens in JWT format by default.
cards.explanation: JWT is the default job-token format. A top-level group can select the legacy format during GitLab 19.x.

cards.statement: GitLab grants extra project permissions to members of projects added to its CI/CD job token allowlist.
cards.explanation: Adding a project to the CI/CD job token allowlist permits token access subject to the user's existing permissions in the target project.
cards.misconception: Adding a project to the allowlist also grants its users permissions in the target project.

cards.statement: GitLab starts a pipeline by default for a successful repository push authenticated with CI_JOB_TOKEN.
cards.explanation: A successful Git push using CI_JOB_TOKEN creates no CI/CD pipeline in the target project.
cards.misconception: A push authenticated with a job token starts a pipeline like a normal push.

cards.statement: A job can set different `aud` values for its named `id_tokens`.
cards.explanation: Each named ID token has its configured audience, so one job can request tokens for different services.

source.title: OpenID Connect (OIDC) Authentication Using ID Tokens

cards.statement: In GitLab Premium and Ultimate, jobs use `secrets` to retrieve values from an external secrets provider.
cards.explanation: A job explicitly requests external secret values with the secrets keyword.

cards.statement: The Maintainer role grants a project member permission to create a project runner.
cards.explanation: GitLab requires the Maintainer role or higher when a project member creates a project runner.

cards.statement: GitLab returns a runner authentication token when a user creates a runner for registration.
cards.explanation: Create the runner first, then register GitLab Runner with the returned runner authentication token.

source.title: Migrating to the new runner registration workflow

cards.statement: A runner matches a tagged job when it shares at least one tag with the job.
cards.explanation: A runner needs every tag the job lists. Sharing just one tag does not satisfy a job's complete tag list.
cards.misconception: Sharing one tag is enough for a runner to accept a job.

cards.statement: A tagged runner can accept untagged jobs when Run untagged jobs is enabled.
cards.explanation: Run untagged jobs lets a runner accept jobs with no tags even when the runner has tags.

cards.statement: Protected runners can execute jobs in pipelines for protected tags.
cards.explanation: A protected tag satisfies a protected runner's ref restriction; the job still has to meet that runner's other selection criteria.

cards.statement: Locking a project runner makes GitLab remove its existing assignments to other projects.
cards.explanation: Locking a project runner retains its current project assignments and prevents enabling it in additional projects.
cards.misconception: Locking a project runner removes existing assignments outside its owner project.

cards.statement: Instance runners use a first in, first out queue to select jobs across projects.
cards.explanation: Instance runners use a fair usage queue, favoring projects with fewer jobs already running.
cards.misconception: Instance runners choose jobs using strict first in, first out ordering.

cards.statement: The Kubernetes executor reuses one Pod for the jobs in the same pipeline stage.
cards.explanation: GitLab Runner asks Kubernetes to create a fresh Pod for each CI/CD job.
cards.misconception: The Kubernetes executor shares one Pod between jobs in the same stage.

cards.statement: `image:docker` configures image options for jobs running with the Kubernetes executor.
cards.explanation: GitLab supports image:docker options with both the Docker and Kubernetes executors.

cards.statement: GitLab Runner applies its `concurrent` limit separately to each runner configuration.
cards.explanation: The concurrent setting caps the combined running jobs across the runner configurations managed by one process.
cards.misconception: Each configured runner has an independent allowance from the global concurrent setting.

cards.statement: GitLab recommends keeping GitLab Runner's major.minor version aligned with GitLab's.
cards.explanation: Matching major.minor versions helps ensure features that need a matching GitLab Runner version work properly.

cards.statement: GitLab.com hosted Linux runners require job authors to declare a runner tag.
cards.explanation: GitLab.com hosted Linux runners accept untagged jobs; a job tag is optional for the default hosted routing.
cards.misconception: Hosted Linux runners accept jobs only when the job specifies a runner tag.
cards.volatilityNote: GitLab.com may change hosted-runner routing and tagging requirements.
